intro: In 1750 almost every person on earth lived under a king, an emperor or a lord, farmed with tools their great-grandparents would have recognized, and expected their children to do the same. By 1914 republics and constitutions had spread across the Atlantic world, machines driven by coal and electricity made most of what people used, cities of a million were common, and a handful of industrial nations ruled most of the planet. No period of similar length had changed human life so much. This unit is about how that happened and who paid for it.

Three revolutions run through these chapters, and they fed each other. Political revolutions, from Philadelphia and Paris to Haiti and Mexico, declared that governments must rest on the consent of the governed and that people have rights simply because they are people. The Industrial Revolution, starting in Britain, put power in machines and moved millions from farms to factories and cities. Then nationalism and imperialism, armed with the new machines and the new wealth, built nations like Germany and Japan and carved up Africa and Asia, until Europe's rivalries locked into the alliances of 1914.

You will read the documents, the numbers and the testimony: a declaration of rights and a woman's answer to it, a coal-output table, a mill child before a committee, a Chinese official's letter to a queen. You will meet people who won, people who lost, and people who were left out and fought their way in. By the end you should be able to explain why the modern world took the shape it did, and to argue, with evidence, about whether the people who made it kept the promises they wrote down.
bigQuestion: Between 1750 and 1914, who gained from revolution, industry and empire, who paid, and did the promise of equal rights reach the people it was written for?

timeline.t: The Declaration of Independence claims that governments rest on the consent of the governed
Watt and Boulton sell their first improved steam engines; Adam Smith publishes The Wealth of Nations
The Bastille falls, nobles give up privileges on August 4, and France declares the Rights of Man
Enslaved people rise in Saint-Domingue; Olympe de Gouges publishes the Rights of Woman
Haiti declares independence; Napoleon crowns himself emperor and issues his law code
Hidalgo's cry in Mexico; Bolívar and San Martín win independence for Spanish South America
The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opens; Britain passes the Factory Act and abolishes slavery
Revolutions sweep Europe; Marx and Engels publish the Communist Manifesto
Rebellion in India ends East India Company rule; the British Crown takes over
The Meiji Restoration begins in Japan; Italy and Germany complete unification
The Berlin Conference sets rules for dividing Africa; no African is invited
Ethiopia defeats Italy at Adwa; alliances harden until a murder in Sarajevo starts a world war

words.d: agreement; the idea that a government is legitimate only if the people accept it
a written set of basic rules that says how a government works and limits its power
to end something completely by law, such as slavery
the belief that a people sharing a language and history should have their own country
in the 1800s, belief in constitutions, elected assemblies and protected individual rights
money or property saved up and used to start or grow a business
a building where many workers use power-driven machines under one owner's control
the growth of cities as people move into them from the countryside
an organization of workers who bargain with an employer as a group
an economy in which private owners invest money, hire workers for wages and sell goods for profit
the policy of one country taking control of other lands and peoples to build an empire
an agreement between countries to help each other, especially in war

test.q: What idea from the Declaration of Independence most directly challenged kings across Europe?
choices: That governments get their power from the consent of the governed
That colonies should pay taxes
That France should help America
That all countries need a navy
test.why: Rule by consent denied that a king held power by birth or by God's choice.

test.q: Why did the Third Estate object to voting by estate in 1789?
choices: It wanted the king to vote
Two small privileged groups could always outvote the vast majority of France
It had fewer deputies than the nobles
It wanted no votes at all
test.why: One vote per estate let the clergy and nobles, about two percent of people, outvote everyone else.

test.q: What did Olympe de Gouges do in 1791?
choices: Led the march on Versailles
Wrote the Napoleonic Code
Published a Declaration of the Rights of Woman answering the Assembly's declaration
Commanded the Haitian army
test.why: She rewrote the 1789 declaration article by article to include women, and was executed in 1793.

test.q: Which was a cause of the Terror of 1793 to 1794?
choices: Peace with all of Europe
Napoleon's coronation
The end of the draft
War and fear of counter-revolution that made critics look like traitors
test.why: Foreign invasion and internal revolt led the Committee of Public Safety to execute thousands of suspected enemies.

test.q: Why was Haiti's revolution unlike any other?
choices: It was led by French generals
It ended without independence
It was the only successful revolution by enslaved people, creating a free nation in 1804
It was recognized at once by every nation
test.why: Half a million enslaved people defeated planters and Napoleon's army and founded Haiti.

test.q: What event in Europe opened the way for independence in Spanish America?
choices: Napoleon's invasion of Spain in 1808
The Congress of Vienna
The revolutions of 1848
The unification of Italy
test.why: With Spain's king removed, colonists formed their own governments and Bolívar and others fought for independence.

test.q: Which set of advantages best explains why Britain industrialized first?
choices: Warm climate and large farms
A strong king and a large army
Cheap coal, available capital, canals and laws protecting property
Colonies in Africa
test.why: Fuel, money, transport and stable law came together in Britain around 1750.

test.q: What did James Watt's separate condenser do?
choices: Made steam engines run on electricity
Cut a steam engine's fuel use to about a quarter, making steam practical for mills
Allowed trains to run at night
Replaced coal with water power
test.why: Keeping the cylinder hot saved most of the fuel earlier engines wasted.

test.q: Why did cholera kill so many in industrial cities?
choices: Because factories were too warm
Because workers ate too little
Because trains brought it from farms
Because drinking water was polluted with sewage in crowded districts without drains
test.why: John Snow's map and later science showed cholera spread through fouled water.

test.q: What principle did Britain's Factory Act of 1833 establish?
choices: That government could regulate work inside factories and enforce it with inspectors
That all children could work any hours
That unions were illegal
That mills must close on Sundays
test.why: Paid inspectors, however few, meant the state had claimed the right to look inside the factory.

test.q: What did Marx predict that did not happen in industrial countries?
choices: That factories would use machines
That cities would grow
That there would be owners and workers
That wages would keep falling until workers overthrew the owners
test.why: Wages in industrial nations rose over the long run, and revolutions in Marx's name came in farming countries.

choices: Through a vote of the Frankfurt parliament
Through three short wars led by Prussia
Through an alliance with Austria and the pope
Through peaceful negotiation with France
test.why: Prussia defeated Denmark, Austria and France, and the German Empire was proclaimed at Versailles in 1871.

test.q: What did Japan and Ethiopia both do in this era?
choices: Became colonies of Britain
Refused all contact with Europe
Built modern armies with weapons bought from Europe and defeated a European power
Joined the Triple Alliance
test.why: Meiji Japan beat Russia in 1905 and Menelik's Ethiopia beat Italy at Adwa in 1896.

test.q: What was decided at the Berlin Conference, and who was missing?
choices: Rules for dividing Africa were set, and no African was present
Africa was declared independent, and Germany was absent
The Congo was given to France, and Britain was absent
Ethiopia was divided, and Italy was absent
test.why: Fourteen European and American states set the terms of the scramble without any African ruler or representative.

test.q: Why did a murder in Sarajevo in 1914 lead to a world war?
choices: Because Serbia invaded Germany
Because the assassin was British
Because the Ottoman Empire declared war on everyone
Because the alliance system and mobilization plans pulled every great power, and their empires, into a Balkan quarrel
test.why: Austria's ultimatum to Serbia triggered promises among allies, and within five weeks all the great powers were at war.

write.prompt: Make a claim: between 1750 and 1914, did the promise of equal rights made in 1776 and 1789 reach the people it left out, or was it mostly broken? Support your claim with evidence from at least two chapters and explain your reasoning.
tips: State your claim in one clear sentence, and say which people you are judging it by: women, the enslaved, workers, colonized peoples.
Use specific evidence: de Gouges, Haiti's independence, the Factory Acts, Chartism, the Berlin Conference, the color line.
Explain your reasoning: show how each piece of evidence supports your claim, not just that it exists.
Take the other side seriously: what would someone who disagrees point to, and why does your evidence outweigh it?
Give dates and eras for every person and event you use.
